theory:
ATOMIC STRUCTURE — KEY THEORY

The atom
- An atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (protons + neutrons) surrounded by electrons in energy levels (shells).
- Proton: charge +1, mass ~1 u.   Neutron: charge 0, mass ~1 u.   Electron: charge -1, mass ~1/1836 u.

Atomic number and mass number
- Atomic number (Z) = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom.
- Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons.
- Number of neutrons = A - Z.

Isotopes
- Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different A).
- They have identical chemical properties (same electron arrangement) but slightly different physical properties.
- Example: 12C, 13C and 14C are isotopes of carbon.

Electronic configuration
- Maximum electrons in shell n = 2n^2  (K=2, L=8, M=18).
- Electrons fill shells from the lowest energy level outwards; the outer shell (valence electrons) controls chemical behaviour.

Exam tips
- Always show working for A - Z calculations.
- In ions, electrons change but protons stay the same (Z never changes).

questions.q: The atomic number of an element is the number of…
questions.d: electrons in the outer shell only
questions.explanation: Atomic number (Z) = number of protons. In a neutral atom it also equals the number of electrons.

questions.q: Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons but different numbers of…
questions.explanation: Isotopes = same Z, different mass numbers, so the neutron count (A - Z) differs.

questions.q: The maximum number of electrons that can occupy the M shell (n = 3) is…
questions.explanation: Maximum capacity = 2n^2 = 2 x 9 = 18.

questions.q: An atom of 23Na (mass number 23, atomic number 11) contains how many neutrons?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = A - Z = 23 - 11 = 12.

questions.q: Which particle has a relative mass of about 1/1836 and a charge of -1?
questions.explanation: The electron is ~1836 times lighter than a proton and carries charge -1.

theory:
CHEMICAL BONDING — KEY THEORY

Why atoms bond
- Atoms bond to achieve a stable (noble gas) electron arrangement — usually a full outer shell (octet / duplet).

Ionic bonding (metal + non-metal)
- Electrons are TRANSFERRED from metal to non-metal, forming cations (+) and anions (-).
- Held by strong electrostatic attraction. e.g. NaCl, MgO, CaCl2.
- Properties: high m.p., crystalline solids, conduct electricity when molten or in solution.

Covalent bonding (non-metal + non-metal)
- Electrons are SHARED in pairs. e.g. H2, Cl2, CH4, CO2.
- A single bond = 1 shared pair; double bond = 2 pairs (O=C=O); triple bond = 3 pairs.
- Simple molecules: low m.p., do not conduct. Giant covalent (diamond, SiO2): very hard, high m.p.

Metallic bonding
- Lattice of metal cations in a 'sea' of delocalised electrons -> conducts electricity and heat; malleable.

Exam tips
- Draw dot-and-cross diagrams with the full outer shell only.
- Remember: MgCl2 needs TWO Cl- ions per Mg2+.

questions.q: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is best described as…
questions.explanation: A metal (Na) + non-metal (Cl) -> electron transfer -> ionic lattice.

questions.q: A covalent bond is formed when atoms…
questions.d: attract by van der Waals forces only
questions.explanation: Covalent = sharing of electron pairs between non-metal atoms.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide (CO2) contains which bonds between carbon and oxygen?
questions.explanation: O=C=O : carbon forms a double bond with each oxygen atom.

questions.q: Which property is typical of an ionic compound?
questions.explanation: Ions are free to move when molten or in solution, so ionic compounds then conduct.

questions.q: Metals conduct electricity because they contain…
questions.explanation: The 'sea' of delocalised electrons carries the current through the metal lattice.

theory:
CHEMICAL CALCULATIONS — THE MOLE TOOLKIT

The core formulas
- n = m / M        (moles = mass in grams / molar mass)
- c = n / V        (concentration in mol dm-3 = moles / volume in dm3)
- n = V / 22.4     (moles of gas = volume in dm3 / 22.4 dm3 mol-1 at STP)
- Number of particles = n x L   (L = Avogadro constant = 6.022 x 10^23 mol-1)

Molar mass
- M of a compound = sum of relative atomic masses. e.g. M(H2O) = 2(1) + 16 = 18 g mol-1.
- Worked example: moles in 36 g of water = m/M = 36/18 = 2 mol.

Concentration
- c = n/V with V in dm3  (1000 cm3 = 1 dm3).
- Worked example: 0.5 mol in 250 cm3 -> V = 0.25 dm3 -> c = 0.5/0.25 = 2 mol dm-3.

Stoichiometry (mole ratios)
- Read the ratio straight from the balanced equation.
- e.g. N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 : 1 mol N2 needs 3 mol H2 and gives 2 mol NH3.

Exam tips
- Convert cm3 to dm3 (divide by 1000) BEFORE using c = n/V.
- Keep 3 significant figures and always write the unit.

questions.q: How many moles are there in 18 g of water? (H = 1, O = 16)
The volume occupied by 1 mole of any gas at STP is…
questions.explanation: Molar gas volume at STP = 22.4 dm3 mol-1.

questions.q: A solution contains 0.25 mol of NaOH in 500 cm3. Its concentration is…
The Avogadro constant is…
questions.explanation: L = 6.022 x 10^23 particles per mole.

questions.q: In the reaction N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, 1 mol of N2 reacts completely with…
questions.explanation: The balanced equation shows the ratio N2 : H2 = 1 : 3.

theory:
ENERGETICS — KEY THEORY

Exothermic vs endothermic
- Exothermic: releases heat to the surroundings, DeltaH is NEGATIVE. e.g. combustion, neutralisation.
- Endothermic: absorbs heat, DeltaH is POSITIVE. e.g. thermal decomposition, photosynthesis.

Enthalpy change (DeltaH)
- DeltaH = H(products) - H(reactants).
- Exothermic pathway: reactants ABOVE products on the energy diagram.
- Activation energy (Ea) = energy from reactants up to the peak (must be supplied to start).

Bond breaking and making
- Breaking bonds ABSORBS energy; making bonds RELEASES energy.
- DeltaH ~ (energy to break bonds) - (energy released making bonds).
- If more energy is released making bonds than used breaking them, the reaction is exothermic.

Calorimetry
- q = mcDeltaT   (m = mass of solution, c = 4.2 J g-1 C-1 for water, DeltaT = temperature change).

Exam tips
- State the sign of DeltaH in every answer.
- A catalyst lowers Ea but does NOT change DeltaH.

questions.q: An exothermic reaction…
questions.a: absorbs heat and has a positive DeltaH
questions.b: releases heat and has a negative DeltaH
questions.d: has products above reactants on the energy diagram
questions.explanation: Exothermic = heat given out, so H(products) < H(reactants) and DeltaH < 0.

questions.q: Bond breaking is always…
questions.explanation: Energy must be supplied to break bonds, so bond breaking is endothermic.

questions.q: The activation energy of a reaction is…
questions.c: the energy needed to reach the top of the energy barrier
questions.d: the energy in one mole of gas at STP
questions.explanation: Ea is the gap from the reactants up to the peak of the energy profile.

questions.q: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by…
questions.d: shifting the equilibrium to the right
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower Ea; DeltaH is unchanged.

questions.q: 50 g of water is heated and its temperature rises by 10 C. Heat absorbed is… (c = 4.2 J g-1 C-1)
questions.explanation: q = mcDeltaT = 50 x 4.2 x 10 = 2100 J.

theory:
CHEMICAL EQUILIBRIUM — KEY THEORY

Dynamic equilibrium
- In a closed system, forward and reverse reactions continue at EQUAL rates; concentrations stay constant.

Le Chatelier's principle
- If a constraint (change of concentration, pressure or temperature) is imposed on a system at equilibrium,
  the system adjusts so as to oppose that constraint.

Predicting the shift
- Concentration: add a reactant -> shifts to the RIGHT (uses it up).
- Pressure (gases only): increase pressure -> shifts to the side with FEWER moles of gas.
- Temperature: increase T -> shifts in the ENDOTHERMIC direction.

The equilibrium constant Kc
- For aA + bB <=> cC + dD :  Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / [A]^a [B]^b
- Kc changes ONLY with temperature.
- Big Kc -> products favoured; small Kc -> reactants favoured.

Industrial example — Haber process
- N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, DeltaH < 0.
- High pressure (~200 atm): more NH3 (fewer gas moles on right).
- Low temperature favours yield but is slow -> compromise ~450 C plus iron catalyst.

Exam tips
- Catalyst does NOT change Kc or the position of equilibrium — it only speeds up attainment.
- Write Kc expressions without solids or pure liquids.

questions.q: At dynamic equilibrium…
questions.c: forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates
questions.d: the products are all used up
questions.explanation: Dynamic = both processes continue, at the same rate, so concentrations stay constant.

questions.q: For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium…
questions.d: only if a catalyst is present
questions.explanation: Right side has 2 moles of gas vs 4 on the left; higher pressure favours the side with fewer moles.

questions.q: Raising the temperature of an exothermic equilibrium shifts it…
questions.explanation: The system opposes the rise by moving in the endothermic (heat-absorbing) direction.

questions.q: The value of Kc for a reaction is changed only by…
questions.explanation: Kc depends only on temperature — concentration, pressure and catalysts do not alter it.
